The case of regular graphs was settled by Fu and Hu [9] using linear forests in the decomposition.
Faudree, Gould, Jacobson, and Lesniak [6] proved the conjecture for mm sufficiently large and GG of maximum degree at most
(2​2−2)​m(2\sqrt{2}-2)m, where the graphs in the decomposition are short paths. This extends a previous result of Fu [8] who proved the conjecture for graphs of degree at most m/2m/2.




Finding ascending decompositions can be difficult and interesting even for rather specific host graphs. For example
Ma, Zhou, and Zhou [19] proved that a star forest with components of size
at least mm has an ascending subgraph decomposition into stars.
Here and throughout the paper, the size of a graph is the number of its edges.
This was previously another conjecture of Alavi, Boals, Chartrand, Erdős, and Oellerman which is appealing due to having an entirely number-theoretic formulation. In this case the problem is equivalent to saying that for any set of numbers a1,…,at≥ma_{1},\dots,a_{t}\geq m with a1+⋯+at=m⁡(m+1)/2a_{1}+\dots+a_{t}=m(m+1)/2 it is possible to decompose the interval [m][m] into sets A1,…,AtA_{1},\dots,A_{t} with the numbers in each AiA_{i} summing to aia_{i}. For a comprehensive survey of prior results in this area we refer the reader to [2, Chapter 8].

We also prove the following statement that may be of independent interest. It says that any graph GG with Θ⁡(m2)\Theta(m^{2}) edges and maximum degree O⁡(m)O(m) can be decomposed into Θ⁡(m)\Theta(m) pairwise isomorphic graphs plus o⁡(m2)o(m^{2}) edges; see Lemma 21.



Notation.




We use standard asymptotic notation throughout. For positive real functions f,gf,g of a positive variable nn we write f=O⁡(g)f=O(g) if the limit lim supn→∞f⁡(n)/g⁡(n)\limsup_{n\to\infty}f(n)/g(n) is finite,
and write f=o⁡(g)f=o(g) if the limit is 00.




Theorem 2 follows by combining Theorem 3 above with Lemma 6 below, which shows that a graph
with (m+12)\binom{m+1}{2} edges and maximum degree O⁡(m)O(m) has an ascending subgraph decomposition (we sometimes abbreviate this to ASD).
Before describing how we deal with each component separately, let us sketch how Theorem 2 follows from Theorem 3 and Lemma 6. First note that Theorem 3 implies the following.

Lemma 6.




Now we sketch the proof that every GG with maximum degree at most O⁡(m)O(m) has an ASD.
The main idea is to almost decompose GG in several stages, so that at each stage the decomposition consists of “nice” graphs which at the very end can be combined to form an ASD.
First, we decompose edges incident to small degree vertices (namely, at most c​mcm for some appropriate constant cc) into isomorphic star forests
and a remainder that has few edges (cf. Lemma 20).
For this step, we first decompose edges with one large degree vertex and one small degree vertex into isomorphic star forests, via Lemma 10, then we decompose edges incident to only small degree vertices via Vizing’s theorem and Lemma 8, and finally we combine the star forests and matchings via Lemma 12.
Second, we almost decompose the edges incident only to large degree vertices into copies of complete bipartite graphs (cf. Lemma 14).
This gives an almost decomposition of GG into isomorphic “forests” whose components are stars and complete bipartite graphs, and each forest contains a large matching (cf. Lemma 21).
